pr_title: Convert Math{F}.CoreCLR methods from FCall to QCall
pr_body:
Fixes #13820

TODOs:

- [x] decide which c-runtime functions to call directly
  * CRT functions are directly registered to QCalls, without the wrappers.
- [x] how to handle `/fp:fast` vs. `/fp:precise` when p/invoking crt functions on Windows
  * remove the wrappers and /fp:fast logic. we will use the default settings of the project (/fp:fast is always on).
pr_comments:
> Convert math intrinsics to named intrinsics

This looks like a signifiant change on its own. Would you mind submitting it in a separate PR to make it easier to review, test and get in?

@jkotas, @tannergooding, in CLR <del>checked</del> debug x64 builds (all platforms), Single API `MathF.Abs(-3.3f)` is returning `-3.3` instead of `3.3`. Other build flavors do not have this issue. Also the double API `Math.Abs(-3.3)` does not has this issue in <del>checked</del> debug build. I couldn't figure out the reason. Is there any special handling for <del>Checked</del> Debug build which I should look into?

Edit: locally, I can only reproduce this issue with CLR's Debug build, but CI encounters in CLR Checked build.

```sh
# repros `MathF.Abs(-3.3f)` issue
./build.sh -c Debug

# do not produce the issue
./build.sh -rc Checked
./build.sh -c Release
```

>  CLR Checked build.

The difference between checked and debug builds are optimizations settings. Debug is asserts on + optimizations off. Checked is assert on + optimizations on.

Remaining failures are related to 'Insert GC Polls', which seems to have recent changes (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/39111).

ARM64 checked tests are failing this assertion: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/c5b39f3b9ac806cb1c03e2779ebef58d3880297e/src/coreclr/src/jit/flowgraph.cpp#L2341-L2342

and x86 checked test is failing this one: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/c5b39f3b9ac806cb1c03e2779ebef58d3880297e/src/coreclr/src/jit/flowgraph.cpp#L4142-L4144

I think we should call CRT functions directly where possible. It should have less overhead than QCall wrappers. It may be worth looking at the compiled code disassembly to see whether it is the case.

> how to handle /fp:fast vs. /fp:precise when p/invoking crt functions on Windows

Does taking address of a math C function take /fp:fast vs. /fp:precise into account?

> Does taking address of a math C function take /fp:fast vs. /fp:precise into account?

It generally does not. The "precise" variant generally calls into the CRT implementation while the fast may compile down to a different intrinsic pattern if the hardware supports it or sometimes a different variant of the CRT function.
It might be worth comparing the disassembly or getting perf measurements to see what the difference between fast and precise is and if it is buying us anything meaningful.

For reference, one example of this difference is with `ceil`: https://godbolt.org/z/K145vG

The "fast" implementation also has a minor bug which is tracked by https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/11003

I think the P/Invoke will use the fp-model of library being invoked, however it was compiled, e.g. with this:

```c#
using System;
using System.Runtime.InteropServices;
public class Program
{
    public static void Main() => Console.Write(ceil(2.3));

    [DllImport("msvcrt.dll")]
    static extern double ceil(double x);
}
```
we cannot control the behavior of `msvcrt.dll`. If we need to be in control of which model to use on Windows (https://github.com/dotnet/coreclr/pull/19725), should we continue with the QCalls?

We need to get some numbers about the performance impact of this change. https://github.com/dotnet/performance has micro-benchmarks that cover this. @tannergooding Do we have any real world math benchmarks that exercise this?

I expected that we will see some extra overhead. It would be useful to see whether the performance can be improved by avoiding the QCall wrappers and referencing the  math functions directly in ecalllist.h.

@jkotas, if we use msvcrt.dll functions directly, we will lose runtime control over /fp:fast, and the corrections carefully made in https://github.com/dotnet/coreclr/pull/19725. Would that be an acceptable breaking change if we get different results?
I think we need data about what we are gaining and losing with each option to decide. I think different, but still correct, result would be ok.

OK. I have ran perf tests with `--filter *MathBenchmark*` using current fcall-to-qcall change. Here are the results: https://gist.github.com/am11/e39ecb16d6f6690597db1ee19a5561ca. There are few small wins, regressions and some remained the same.

I will work on direct P/Invoke next.

@jkotas, I pushed a commit on PR branch then created a new branch from it, as the performance regression in FCall to P/Invoke is more prominent compared to FCall to QCall: https://github.com/am11/runtime/commit/a71c577eef84c8101ff26383e28e26ff8735cdb3. Benchmark results at: https://gist.github.com/am11/3de081aaa48e48ec69ca08272b2ba429
Was `[SuppressGCTransitionAttribute]` needed on non-QCall DllImports?

> Was [SuppressGCTransitionAttribute] needed on non-QCall DllImports?

Yes. `[SuppressGCTransitionAttribute]` is needed if you are experimenting with changing these into non-QCall DllImports.

QCall mapping can point directly to C runtime function. It may easier to do it this way than via non-QCall DllImports. For example:

```
< QCFuncElement("AcoshInternal", COMDouble::AcoshInternal)
> QCFuncElement("AcoshInternal", acosh)
```

Results, all with `[SuppressGCTransition]` attribute:

* FCall to QCall (indirect): https://gist.github.com/am11/e39ecb16d6f6690597db1ee19a5561ca
* FCall to QCall (direct): https://gist.github.com/am11/26d8e8ff43fc3cc537f45adb7591fdcf
* FCall to non-QCall DllImport: https://gist.github.com/am11/8dcbea6e3ca864585f14f888d10953e3

Going by the sum of Ratio columns:

```javascript
// JavaScript, run in browser console of gist links

// base
[...document.querySelectorAll('table tr:nth-child(3n+1):not(:nth-child(3n+2)) td:nth-child(10)')]
  .map(subject => parseFloat(subject.textContent))
  .reduce((subjectA, subjectB) => subjectA + subjectB)

// vs.
// PR
[...document.querySelectorAll('table tr:nth-child(3n+2):not(:nth-child(3n+1)) td:nth-child(10)')]
  .map(subject => parseFloat(subject.textContent))
  .reduce((subjectA, subjectB) => subjectA + subjectB)
```

* FCall to QCall (indirect): 30 vs. 34.28
* FCall to QCall (direct): 30 vs. 32.57000000000001
* FCall to non-QCall DllImport: 30 vs. 31.759999999999998

All are slight regressions compared to FCall.
non-QCall DllImport is the best among the regressions (https://github.com/am11/runtime/commit/e8c4c318d9030ecc5a5091ced0e4b9e73dcbe43b).
Did you have a chance to look at the disassembly for the cases that show the largest regressions? Is there anything that can be improved?

> Do we have any real world math benchmarks that exercise this?

Not that I am aware of. Many of the mathematically intensive benchmarks are using things like intrinsics and computing a "good enough" sin/cos/tan (since they are largely graphics related).

We do have simple tests covering each of the math functions which should accurately show the perf difference on a per-function basis.

> we will lose runtime control over /fp:fast, and the corrections carefully made in

I would think the best thing is to:
* Measure the existing code from master
* Measure the existing code from master with the fp:fast pragma removed

This will give an accurate baseline over what perf loss, if any, we can expect from this switch.
Windows is currently the only thing that fp:fast impacts, and so it may start reporting more accurate results that are more inline with Linux/macOS which might be beneficial anyways.

We can then separately decide which of QCALL, P/Invoke, or another alternative is appropriate based on the perf difference against whichever of the above two we decide upon.

issue_context.title: Calling System.Math floating point operations in a loop causes long GC pause times

review_comments: The intrinsic attribute should stay on the public entrypoint.

Thanks for the catch. Although with:

```c#
 #pragma warning disable CA1401 // P/Invokes should not be visible 
```
it compiled (and normally works with regular P/Invoke), but checked builds were raising this assert for QCall: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/867ad8d20402e3bee580e0af6577f87912103c78/src/coreclr/src/vm/ecall.cpp#L724
This was the main reason of defining *Internal variants.
The comment in front the QCall assert talks about Code-Access-Security that is not relevant in .NET Core. But it think it may be still a good idea to avoid exporting DllImports directly.

`EntryPoint` does not get registered with QCalls; as in:

```c#
[DllImport(RuntimeHelpers.QCall, CallingConvention = CallingConvention.Cdecl, EntryPoint = "AbsF")]
public static float Abs(float value);
```
with:
```c++
QCFuncElement("AbsF", fabsf)
```
it continues to match by method name, and silently uses double `QCFuncElement("Abs", fabs)`, which later results in test failures. Changed this one to call private method.
